data.title: Middle East Eye: Trump lands in China for meeting with Xi and Putin
data.author: Oscar Rickett
data.summary:
Trump lands in China for meeting with Xi and Putin
US President Donald Trump has arrived in China for the Apec summit in Shenzhen, where he is expected to meet with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladmir Putin.
The historic trilateral meeting between the leaders will take place on Thursday. Xi, Trump and Putin are due to meet on the sidelines of the summit to potentially discuss Russia's war with Ukraine and the US-Israeli war on Iran, as well as trade, AI and nuclear weapons.
Xi met Trump off the plane on the tarmac at Shenzhen, reciprocating Trump's gesture when the Chinese leader visited the US in September.
Xi told Trump he hoped their talks would help advance a “constructive, strategic and stable relationship” between China and the US, based on “respect, fairness and reciprocity”, according to China’s state news agency Xinhua.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said that Putin and Trump are unlikely to have time for fully fledged bilateral negotiations in China, but may talk on the event's sidelines, the Tass news agency reported.
Peskov was cited as saying that the two leaders would exchange views on the conflicts in Ukraine and Iran if they got a chance to talk one-on-one.
US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping (Reuters)

data.title: Middle East Eye: Somalia's president accuses UAE of 'interference' in his country
data.author: Oscar Rickett
data.summary:
Somalia's president accuses UAE of 'interference' in his country
The president of Somalia has accused the United Arab Emirates of "interference" in his country's internal affairs.
Speaking in a televised address, Hassan Sheikh Mohamud said the UAE had established a military presence, including bases, outside Mogadishu’s national security framework without the government's approval.
He said the country had also funded armed groups and opponents of the central government.
"Somalia is not a thoroughfare to be traversed illegally - it is not a commodity to be bought, nor is it a place that one can enter or leave at will," Hassan Sheikh said.
Tensions between the UAE and Somalia have been high for many years, in part due to the former's support for the breakaway nation of Somaliland.

data.title: Middle East Eye: Trump's Board of Peace says Gaza ceasefire has delivered 'nothing visible'
data.author: Oscar Rickett
data.summary:
Trump's Board of Peace says Gaza ceasefire has delivered 'nothing visible'
US President Donald Trump's Board of Peace, the body supposedly tasked with overseeing the end to fighting in Gaza, has accused both Israel and Hamas of failing to end hostilities, leaving the Palestinian enclave's population in dire need.
The 12-page Board of Peace report, seen by Reuters, is the body's second to the United Nations Security Council since the US-backed ceasefire came into effect 13 months ago. It offers a "sobering assessment of progress made since then", Reuters said.
The board, established and headed by Trump, is expected to present the report's findings to a meeting of the council in New York at the end of November.
“The distance between what has been agreed and what is happening on the ground nonetheless remains the principal risk to the process,” the report said, warning that “a ceasefire that delivers nothing visible cannot be sustained indefinitely.”
Since the ceasefire, Israeli attacks have killed more than 1,431 people, including at least 300 children, and wounded 5,026.
The office of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and a spokesperson for the political office of Hamas did not immediately respond to requests for comment on the report.
“There is no ceasefire in Gaza. People talk about a ceasefire but at best it’s a reduced fire,” Chris Sidoti, a member of the UN Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory, told MEE's Expert Witness podcast this week.

data.title: Middle East Eye: Israel launches assault targeting residential areas in Gaza despite ceasefire
data.author: Oscar Rickett
data.summary:
Israel launches assault targeting residential areas in Gaza despite ceasefire
The Israeli military launched a new ground assault on residential areas in the central Gaza Strip on Wednesday, forcing displaced Palestinian families to flee despite the ceasefire agreement.
Tanks were seen advancing into areas near the Bureij and Nuseirat refugee camps, according to local media.
At least two people were wounded by indiscriminate fire near Nuseirat refugee camp, while scores of residents fled the area following the surprise assault.
The Israeli military confirmed the attack, which is taking place beyond the so-called "Yellow Line" – a military boundary imposed by Israeli forces inside the Gaza Strip following the October 2025 ceasefire agreement.
The army claimed it was targeting "terrorist infrastructure" in areas it designated as “Blocks 660, 661 and 666”. These are residential areas where Palestinian residents and displaced families live.

India has signed a contract worth 19.76bn rupees ($211.48m) with Israel Aerospace Industries for the upgradation and obsolescence management of Barak Point Defence Missile System for the Indian navy, the Indian defence ministry said in a statement on Wednesday.
Israel Aerospace Industries is Israel's largest state-owned aerospace and defence manufacturer. The company makes multiple weapons systems specifically for the Israeli military, including the Heron TP killer drone.

The Barak Point Defence Missile System is marketed as a "combat proven" defence "against drones, aircraft, cruise missiles and tactical ballistic missiles".

data.title: Middle East Eye: Labour MPs quit Somaliland group over Israel and chair’s ties to far-right Restore
data.author: Oscar Rickett
data.summary:
Labour MPs quit Somaliland group over Israel and chair’s ties to far-right Restore
Kim Johnson, an MP from the UK’s Labour Party, was helping to host an event in the UK parliament marking the anniversary of Somaliland’s self-declared independence when she was told that an official from another government was on their way to attend.
“When I heard there would be an Israeli government official there, I just left the event as quickly as I could,” Johnson told Middle East Eye.
The unexpected appearance of an Israeli official at the May event was the final straw for Johnson, a backbencher on Labour’s left and an advocate for Palestinian rights, who quit the UK’s all-party parliamentary group (APPG) on Somaliland soon after.
Abtisam Mohamed, the Labour MP for Sheffield Central and Johnson’s deputy in the group, also resigned her post this week, Middle East Eye can reveal, while Kerry McCarthy, Labour MP for Bristol East, has stopped participating in the group’s activities until its chair, the Conservative MP Gavin Williamson, resigns.
MEE understands that the APPG, Westminster’s main forum advocating for Somaliland and its diaspora, has not met since before the UK parliament’s summer recess amid fallout over Israel's recognition of Somaliland and Williamson's ties to the hardline anti-immigration party Restore Britain.

Submitted by

Riyadh faces a complex dilemma: protecting its Yemeni allies and shielding its own economy have become increasingly difficult to reconcile
Armoured vehicles are left by the sea as Saudi-backed forces sustain losses against Yemen’s Houthis, in this screengrab from 16 November 2026 (Ansar Allah Military Media/Handout via Reuters)
Off
The forces that were supposed to recover Yemen’s western coast are now concentrating on defending Aden. That reversal captures the scale of Saudi Arabia’s predicament.
Southern forces fighting alongside Yemen’s internationally recognised government this week announced their withdrawal from positions around Bab al-Mandab and Dhubab. Their stated priority was to secure Aden and neighbouring governorates.
A six-week counteroffensive had failed to reverse the Houthis’ coastal gains, as the government’s political centre took precedence over the maritime corridor its supporters had sought to recover.
Meanwhile, military and government sources told the AFP news agency that Houthi fighters had reached positions approximately 60 kilometres from Aden.
The city’s fall is neither established nor inevitable. But the threat already produces consequences: it changes where government forces deploy, what Saudi Arabia must defend, and the terms on which the next round of negotiations could begin.
The current offensive connects battles that might appear separate on a map. The Houthis advanced roughly 150 kilometres along the Red Sea coast in a week in September, capturing Mokha and reaching Bab al-Mandab. The element of surprise, and relatively centralised command, helped them exploit divisions among their opponents.
Progress became harder as fighting moved towards the Taiz-Lahij highlands, where local resistance strengthened and the terrain complicated further advances.

data.title: Middle East Eye: 'I still love you, pal,' Biden told Netanyahu in final phone call
data.author: Oscar Rickett
data.summary:
'I still love you, pal,' Biden told Netanyahu in final phone call
In his last phone call with Benjamin Netanyahu as US president, Joe Biden told the Israeli prime minister, "I still love you, pal", according to a transcript of the conversation obtained by the Jerusalem Post.
Five days before leaving office, Biden told Netanyahu, "You're a good man", and "I admire you."
“You’ve been through hell. I can’t tell you how much I appreciate you and what you’ve been through,” Biden said, according to the transcript. “I know we’ve disagreed on occasion but, you know… I still love you, pal.”
The then-US president continued: “I don’t know how you’ve done it all… Next time I think I have a tough job, I’ll think of you… you’re a good man… I admire you. It took a lot of courage to do what you did.”
The call took place on 15 January 2025, the day a ceasefire and hostage-release agreement between Israel and Hamas was announced.
The transript appears to clash with Biden's own account of his relationship with Netanyahu in his memoir Promise Me, America , which has just been published.
In excerpts reported by Newsweek, the former president accused Netanyahu of having “Trump-like tendencies” and “bending democratic institutions to serve his personal needs.” Biden also described a lack of trust between them and criticised Netanyahu’s attempt to overhaul Israel’s judiciary.

data.title: Middle East Eye: Amnesty calls for RSF drone strikes on el-Obeid to be investigated as war crimes
data.author: Oscar Rickett
data.summary:
Amnesty calls for RSF drone strikes on el-Obeid to be investigated as war crimes
Amnesty International called on Wednesday for Rapid Support Forces (RSF) drone strikes on el-Obeid in Sudan's North Kordofan state to be investigated as war crimes.
The strikes have hit residential areas and civil infrastructure across the city and its surroundings, killing dozens and disrupting public services.
Amnesty investigated nine RSF drone strikes in el-Obeid and its surroundings, which killed 37 civilians and injured 10 between June and August 2026.
Three of the strikes hit residential areas and four struck key civilian infrastructure, including el-Obeid’s power plant, fuel stations, and the main market. Two targeted moving vehicles in the strategically vital city, which sits on the main route between the capital Khartoum and Darfur in the west.
In all incidents, interviewees told Amnesty they either saw or heard the drones, moments before or after the strikes. Amnesty International’s investigation did not identify military objectives in the vicinity of the sites at the time they were struck.

Israeli settlers have established an outpost in a Palestinian-administered area of the occupied West Bank, with the military yet to remove them, Haaretz reported on Wednesday.
According to the report, settlers established a branch of the Homesh yeshiva near the Palestinian village of Yasid, northwest of Nablus, seizing land belonging to the village in Area A.
Under the 1990s Oslo Accords, the occupied West Bank was divided into three areas: Area A, under Palestinian civil and security control; Area B, under Palestinian civil and Israeli security control; and Area C, under full Israeli control.
The Israeli military told Haaretz that it had previously evacuated the outpost, but settlers had since re-established it.
"Entry into Area A is prohibited by law, dangerous to civilians and constitutes a criminal offence," an Israeli army spokesperson said.
"The outpost was evacuated once," the spokesperson said, adding that enforcement efforts against illegal settlements in the West Bank "continue at all times".
However, the military did not say whether it intended to remove the outpost again.
Ras Abu Nimel, a Palestinian landowner in the area, told Haaretz that settlers had seized land designated for a new residential neighbourhood, halting the project.
"Everything was ready for the start of marketing the plots, but the settlers’ takeover halted the project," Abu Nimel said. He estimated that settlers had seized around 15 dunams of land belonging to several villages.

The Prisoners’ Media Office said on Tuesday that the prison administration had ordered female detainees to remove their hijabs before being photographed, claiming the procedure was necessary to update their personal records.
Women who refused were physically assaulted.
According to the office, prison staff removed detainees from their cells one by one and took them to a photography room. Those who refused to remove their hijabs were beaten in an attempt to force them to comply.
In one incident, the prison director forcibly removed a detainee’s hijab, slapped her and pushed her into the photography room.
The assault reportedly took place shortly after the woman had completed eight days in solitary confinement.
Amani Sarahneh, a spokesperson for the Palestinian Prisoners’ Club, said lawyers who visited detainees at Damon Prison confirmed that women had been coerced into removing their hijabs during photography procedures.
She added that this was not the first time female detainees had faced such practices.
'Violations are no longer limited to the hijab; they encompass all aspects of life inside the prison'
- Amani Sarahneh, Palestinian Prisoners’ Club

data.title: Middle East Eye: Jordan gets $6.7bn funding for water desalination project
data.author: Oscar Rickett
data.summary:
Jordan gets $6.7bn funding for water desalination project
A desalination project in water-poor Jordan has drawn investment of $6.7bn and talks are underway to launch similar projects in Syria and Yemen, the head of the UN's Green Climate Fund told Reuters on Wednesday.
The project is the biggest commitment yet by the world's largest multilateral climate fund. It aims to address water stress at a time when the climate crisis is increasing the problem.
Jordan ranks among the countries with the least available water.
Launched officially on Wednesday by Prince Faisal bin Al Hussein, the younger brother of Jordan's King Abdullah II, the Aqaba–Amman Water Desalination and Conveyance Project will eventually move 300 million cubic metres of additional water and serve 40 percent of the population.
Last year, the fund approved $295m in grants and loans that attracted further public and private sector funding to reach a total of $6.7bn.
The Green Climate Fund was set up under the United Nations climate framework to help developing nations adapt and curb their emissions.

Permanent Representative of the UAE to the United Nations Ambassador Lana Nusseibeh speaks during a meeting at the UN Headquarters in New York City, 23 February 2023 (AFP)

Will any permanent member of the United Nations Security Council veto the Emirati candidate from becoming the next secretary-general?
Lana Nusseibeh has denied the UN’s own findings about the UAE’s role in Sudan’s brutal civil war but remains a contender to lead the organisation.
On Thursday the Security Council is set to hold its next straw poll on the eight candidates vying to succeed Antonio Guterres, whose term ends on 31 December, as the secretary-general.
It is an informal, anonymous poll on whether members encourage, discourage or have no opinion about a candidate.
Most of the international controversy over the contest for the world body’s highest administrative role has concerned the candidacy of Nusseibeh, a veteran Emirati diplomat.
That's largely due to the United Arab Emirates' role in Sudan’s civil war, where it is accused of supporting the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) - whose mass killings UN investigators say bear the “hallmarks of genocide”.
There is widespread public evidence, including extensive reporting by Middle East Eye, linking the UAE with the supply of arms and other goods to the RSF - although the Emirati government, including Nusseibeh herself, have repeatedly denied it.
The Security Council’s five permanent members - the US, UK, France, China and Russia - are the only countries that can veto candidates.
But diplomatic sources have told MEE that Nusseibeh now has the backing of all five of the members.

Somalia's President, Hassan Sheikh Mohamud, stands at the podium during a handover ceremony at the Mogadishu palace on 23 May 2022 (Hasan Ali Elmi/AFP)

Somalia's president accused the United Arab Emirates of "interference" in his country's internal affairs, and alleged Abu Dhabi was backing armed groups and fuelling divisions between the federal government and regional administrations.
In a 15-minute televised address on Tuesday, Hassan Sheikh Mohamud said the UAE had broken trust between the two countries by establishing military bases and security structures outside of Mogadishu's national command, and was supporting political opponents of the central government.
"I am speaking to you today about the danger this poses to our statehood, because remaining silent would be betrayal," he said.
Mohamud said Somalia had long regarded the UAE as a brotherly country, bound by shared religious, cultural and historical ties, but years of Emirati interference had damaged that relationship.
"We saw them as brothers. We opened our doors to them. We trusted them greatly," he said.
The president, who sharply criticised the UAE in an interview last month, also accused Abu Dhabi of striking agreements with regional administrations over strategic infrastructure without the approval of the federal government in Mogadishu.
He singled out deals concerning the ports of Berbera, Bosaso and Kismayo, arguing that they were national assets belonging to all Somalis and could not be subject to deals that bypassed the central authorities.
"A brother does not burn your house. A brother does not buy your property without your knowledge. A brother does not divide your family," he said.
